conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you so much for making time today. I’m Dr. Maya Collins, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works closely with new mothers. My job is simply to listen, without judgment, and to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

In front of us we have the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a 10-item questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s just a quick way to see how we can best support you right now.

Everything you share stays between you and the clinical team unless you tell us someone is in danger or you need urgent help. We’ll go at your pace; each question can be re-phrased if anything feels confusing. When we’re done, we’ll add up the responses and talk through what they might mean and what next steps—if any—could be helpful.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[soft sigh, eyes downcast]

I… I want to look forward to things, but it feels like the color’s been drained out of everything. Like, my sister keeps saying, “Let’s watch that show we used to love,” and I say yes because I *should* want to, but when it’s on I’m just staring at the screen feeling… flat. Even the smell of my morning coffee—usually my little treat—barely registers. I still go through the motions, but the actual *enjoyment* part… most of it is gone.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile that fades quickly]

I’ve laughed a couple of times—like yesterday when the baby let out this tiny burp that sounded like a squeaky toy—but it feels… thin? Like the laugh barely reaches my stomach before it dies out. Most of the time I can tell something is supposed to be funny, but I’m just too tired or heavy to really feel it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shakes head slowly]

Honestly? Hardly at all this week. I keep telling myself, “Tomorrow you’ll want to go for that walk” or “You used to love brunch—maybe next week,” but when the moment comes, it’s like I’m stuck behind a pane of glass watching other people enjoy things. I still *do* stuff, but the looking-forward part feels broken.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice drops, eyes sting with tears]

All the time. Yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “If I were a better mom I’d know the exact routine, the exact song, the exact way to hold him.” When he finally cried himself to sleep I sat on the floor convinced it was because I’m doing everything wrong. I tell myself I’m being stupid, but the guilt just sits on my chest like a weight.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day this week. My mind keeps spinning worst-case scenes—like what if he spits up while I’m dozing and chokes, or what if the rash on his neck is something awful I haven’t spotted? I check his breathing a dozen times a night, even when he’s peacefully asleep. There’s no real reason, but I can’t turn the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[twists the edge of her sweater]

Yeah… a few times. It hits out of nowhere—my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air, even when the baby’s fine and the apartment’s quiet. Last night I was warming a bottle and suddenly pictured him not waking up; my hands shook so hard I nearly dropped it. It passes after a bit, but in the moment it feels like something terrible is about to happen and I’m the only one who sees it coming.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]

Most days, yeah. It’s like I’m wading through waist-deep water—every small task, folding a load of onesies or answering a text, feels twice as heavy. I’ll start the laundry and then just stand in front of the washer thinking, “I can’t do all of this.” I still manage the basics, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[eyes redden]

That’s been the worst part. I finally get him down, but then my head won’t shut off—every tiny mistake I made today loops on repeat. I lie there exhausted yet wide-awake, listening to the monitor, checking the clock every hour. Some nights I drift off around three, then jolt up at five sure I’ve heard him cry even when he’s still asleep. I’m running on fumes.
I have felt sad or miserable

[presses lips together, nodding]

Yeah… most of the week. It’s like a gray fog that just sits there. I’ll be feeding him and tears start slipping down for no clear reason, or I’ll catch my reflection and think, “This is supposed to be the happy time,” and the sadness feels even heavier. It’s not every single minute, but it’s definitely the background music lately.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, voice thick]

A few times. Like the other night—everything was technically fine, he’d finally gone to sleep, but I just sat on the couch and started sobbing. It felt like the sadness had nowhere else to go. Sometimes it’s quiet tears while I’m rocking him; sometimes it’s full-on, can’t-catch-my-breath crying when my partner’s in the other room. It’s not every day, but it’s been happening more than I’d like to admit.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes widening]

No—never. I’ve felt low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

You have shared that over the past week motherhood often feels colorless and heavy; brief smiles fade quickly, the future holds little sparkle, and you carry a steady ache of <sym>guilt</sym> and <sym>worry</sym>. Even simple tasks feel like wading through water, your nights are filled with restless checking on your baby, and tears arrive without clear reason. Despite these struggles you remain devoted to your little one and have not thought of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only brief, superficial laughter that quickly fades; she recognizes humor but cannot fully feel it, matching 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Hardly at all" and describes inability to anticipate pleasure, matching the highest-score option.</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses pervasive self-blame and guilt "all the time" with specific examples, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, uncontrollable worries every day, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with racing heart, shortness of breath, and catastrophic thoughts occurring multiple times, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed on most days, struggling with everyday tasks, but still managing basics—aligns with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty sleeping due to unhappiness/racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the week" with spontaneous crying and persistent low mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes repeated crying episodes that are increasing in frequency and intensity, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 on the EPDS (items scored 0-3) falls well above the ≥14 threshold for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse the two cardinal <med>DSM-5 criteria</medi>: depressed mood and markedly diminished interest/pleasure nearly every day, plus multiple associated features such as <sym>excessive self-blame</sym>, recurrent <sym>panic sensations</sym>, difficulty sleeping even when the baby sleeps, and subjective difficulty coping. This pattern indicates an urgent need for clinical assessment and possible treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health team this week
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks and benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these EPDS results and your daily mood log with your provider
4. Enlist trusted family or friends to help with night shifts so you can obtain 4-hour stretches of sleep
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress
6. Call 911 or your local emergency number if you ever feel you might act on thoughts of self-harm
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood (informal, not diagnostic)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, feelings of “gray fog”  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (“stuck behind a pane of glass”)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding parenting adequacy  
- Daily, non-specific anxiety and intrusive worst-case fears about infant safety  
- Episodic panic sensations (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “wading through water”  
- Sleep disturbance linked to ruminating and hourly infant checks  
- Crying spells with no clear trigger  
- Fatigue despite technically adequate rest periods  

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days over the past week, causing subjective impairment in coping with routine infant-care tasks. No anhedonia totalis—brief amusement reported—but pleasure is fleeting. No self-harm ideation; protective factor noted.

Screening significance  
Findings consistent with elevated risk for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and co-occurring anxiety features; meets threshold for formal follow-up assessment (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9, GAD-7). No immediate safety concerns voiced.

Next step  
Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialist for comprehensive evaluation and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
